query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the alloy’s high configurational entropy drives the formation of a single‐phase, homogeneous oxide during high‐temperature exposure (>900 °C). This uniform oxide phase accommodates thermal expansion with minimal mismatch stress, thereby remaining coherent and protective; in contrast, alloys with lower effective configurational entropy (e.g., multiphase alloys) develop heterogeneous oxide scales that are prone to cracking or spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX alloy in a metallic solid‐solution state (either a single-phase homogeneous structure or a multiphase structure)
generation.intervention: Exposure to temperatures above 900 °C in a controlled oxidative or corrosive atmosphere
generation.conditions: Temperature above 900 °C, sustained exposure in a defined gaseous environment (e.g., air or simulated corrosive gas), with comparison between single-phase and multiphase alloy states
generation.structural_mediator: The degree of configurational disorder (entropy) within the alloy, which governs the uniformity of the cation distribution in the forming oxide
generation.mechanism: Highly disordered cationic distributions stabilize a uniform, single-phase oxide lattice that minimizes internal stresses due to reduced grain-boundary density and lower thermal expansion mismatch. In contrast, alloys with less configurational entropy (or multiphase structures) form oxides with multiple phases and interfaces, which promote stress concentrations and crack initiation that can lead to spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys exhibiting a high-entropy, single-phase solid-solution state will form a continuous, adherent, coherent oxide layer that remains stable during high-temperature exposure, whereas multiphase variants will form nonuniform, cracked oxides that spall under similar conditions.
generation.baseline: A controlled comparison against an alloy system of similar base composition (e.g., CrFeCoNi without the additional X element or a multiphase variant) known to form heterogeneous oxides under high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected for exposures above 900 °C in oxidative/corrosive atmospheres; the influence of the additional X element (Si, Mn, or Al) and the single- versus multiphase nature of the alloy are the critical compositional/structural boundaries.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative impact of each X element (Si, Mn, or Al) on the oxide phase formation and stress accommodation is not fully established; additional kinetic factors during oxidation may also contribute to the process, and their roles remain to be quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a set of CrFeCoNiX samples with controlled single-phase and multiphase microstructures. Subject both sets to high-temperature exposure (>900 °C) in a controlled oxidative atmosphere. Use microscopy (SEM/TEM) and phase analysis (XRD) to compare the oxide layers formed on each microstructure over time.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and uniformity (via SEM/TEM)
Phase composition of the oxide (via XRD)
Integrity tests (adhesion and crack density measurements)
Thermal cycling stability (to assess persistent coherence)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both the single-phase and multiphase alloys develop oxide scales with statistically equivalent uniformity, adhesion, and resistance to cracking/spallation under identical exposure conditions, the hypothesis that configurational entropy governs protective oxide formation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Entropy-stabilized oxides

Abstract: Configurational disorder can be compositionally engineered into mixed oxide by populating a single sublattice with many distinct cations. The formulations promote novel and entropy-stabilized forms of crystalline matter where metal cations are incorporated in new ways. Here, through rigorous experiments, a simple thermodynamic model, and a five-component oxide formulation, we demonstrate beyond reasonable doubt that entropy predominates the thermodynamic landscape, and drives a reversible solid-state transformation between a multiphase and single-phase state. In the latter, cation distributions are proven to be random and homogeneous. The findings validate the hypothesis that deliberate configurational disorder provides an orthogonal strategy to imagine and discover new phases of crystalline matter and untapped opportunities for property engineering. The composition of oxide compounds controls many of their properties and electronic phases. Here, the authors show that entropy and configurational disorder can stabilize new phases of oxides, potentially enabling a better engineering of their properties.
